title: Natural Language Processing
text:
Natural Language Processing

Natural Language Processing, commonly abbreviated as NLP, is a subfield of computer science and artificial intelligence that focuses on enabling computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language. Human languages such as English, Spanish, or Mandarin are highly irregular and context-dependent, which makes them fundamentally different from the structured, unambiguous languages that computers were originally designed to process, such as programming languages.

The roots of NLP trace back to the 1950s, when early researchers explored whether machines could translate text between languages or engage in basic conversation. Early systems relied heavily on hand-written rules: a linguist or programmer would encode grammatical rules and dictionaries directly into the software. This rule-based approach worked for narrow, controlled situations but struggled badly with the sheer variety and ambiguity of real language.

Over the following decades, the field shifted toward statistical methods. Instead of hand-coding rules, researchers built systems that learned patterns from large collections of real text, called corpora. This statistical era made tasks like machine translation and speech recognition dramatically more practical, since the system could improve simply by being shown more data rather than requiring a human to write more rules.

The most recent shift, beginning in the 2010s, has been toward deep learning and, more specifically, neural network architectures called transformers. These models learn rich, flexible representations of language directly from massive amounts of text, and they now form the backbone of nearly all modern NLP systems, including translation tools, chatbots, and question answering systems.

NLP is generally divided into two broad directions: natural language understanding (NLU), which focuses on extracting meaning from text, and natural language generation (NLG), which focuses on producing fluent, coherent text as output. A generative question answering system, like the one built in this project, relies on both: it must understand what a user is asking, and then generate a natural-language answer in response.

Typical NLP tasks include text classification (sorting text into categories), named entity recognition (identifying names of people, places, or organizations), sentiment analysis (judging whether text expresses a positive or negative opinion), machine translation, summarization, and question answering. Each of these tasks has its own challenges, but they increasingly share the same underlying technology: large neural language models trained on text.

Despite enormous progress, NLP systems still face real limitations. They can struggle with sarcasm, ambiguity, rare languages or dialects, and situations that require common-sense reasoning outside the text they were trained on. Modern generative systems can also produce fluent-sounding but factually incorrect statements, a problem known as hallucination, which is a central concern for anyone building a trustworthy question answering system.

title: Tokenization
text:
Tokenization

Tokenization is the process of breaking a piece of text into smaller units called tokens, which a computer program can then process one at a time. It is usually the very first step in any natural language processing pipeline, because raw text arrives as an unbroken string of characters, and a model needs some way to divide that string into meaningful pieces before it can do anything useful with it.

The simplest form of tokenization splits text on whitespace and punctuation, treating each word as a token. For example, the sentence "NLP is fascinating!" would be split into the tokens "NLP", "is", "fascinating", and "!". This word-level approach is easy to understand, but it runs into problems with languages that do not use spaces between words, with made-up or rare words, and with the sheer size of the vocabulary it produces, since every distinct word form needs its own entry.

Modern transformer-based models typically use a more sophisticated approach called subword tokenization. Instead of treating whole words as the smallest unit, these methods break rare or complex words into smaller, more frequent pieces. For example, the word "tokenization" itself might be split into pieces like "token" and "ization". Common words remain a single token, while rare or unfamiliar words are represented as a sequence of smaller, familiar subword pieces. This keeps the vocabulary size manageable while still allowing the model to represent virtually any word, including ones it has never seen before, by combining known subword pieces.

Popular subword tokenization algorithms include Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE), WordPiece, and SentencePiece. Each works slightly differently, but they share the same core idea: build a vocabulary of subword units by starting from individual characters and progressively merging the most frequently occurring pairs, until a target vocabulary size is reached.

Tokenization matters for a generative question answering system in several practical ways. First, the length limit of a language model is usually measured in tokens, not words or characters, so understanding tokenization helps explain why very long documents or contexts sometimes get cut off. Second, the way a question is tokenized can affect how well the model understands it, particularly for unusual technical terms, misspellings, or code snippets. Finally, when we talk about "chunking" a document for retrieval, the chunk size is also typically measured in tokens rather than raw characters, which is why tokenization is one of the first concepts to understand before working with chunking or embeddings.

title: Word and Sentence Embeddings
text:
Word and Sentence Embeddings

An embedding is a way of representing a piece of text, whether a single word or an entire sentence, as a list of numbers called a vector. This numerical representation allows a computer to work with the meaning of language mathematically, rather than treating text as an opaque sequence of characters.

The key idea behind embeddings is that words or sentences with similar meanings should end up with similar vectors. If we imagine each vector as a point in a high-dimensional space, then words like "king" and "queen" would land close together, while a word like "banana" would land far away from both. This closeness in the vector space is what lets a computer measure semantic similarity: how alike two pieces of text are in meaning, not just in spelling.

Early word embedding methods, such as Word2Vec and GloVe, learned a single fixed vector for each word by analyzing which words tend to appear near each other across a huge collection of text. These methods captured surprisingly rich relationships. A famous example is that the vector arithmetic "king minus man plus woman" produces a vector very close to "queen," showing that the embedding space had implicitly learned something about gender and royalty.

A major limitation of these early methods was that each word had only one vector, regardless of context. The word "bank" would have the same embedding whether it appeared in "river bank" or "savings bank." Modern transformer-based models solve this by producing contextual embeddings: the vector for a word changes depending on the sentence it appears in, because the model considers the surrounding words when generating the representation.

Sentence embeddings extend this same idea to entire sentences or paragraphs, producing a single vector that represents the overall meaning of a longer piece of text. This is especially important for retrieval-augmented generation systems, where we need to compare the meaning of a user's question against the meaning of many stored passages, in order to find which passages are actually relevant.

Two pieces of text that are worded very differently but mean the same thing, such as "What is NLP?" and "Explain natural language processing," should produce sentence embeddings that are very close together in vector space, even though they share almost no words in common. This is the property that makes embeddings so useful for semantic search: they let a system understand what a question means, rather than just matching keywords.

title: Transformers and the Attention Mechanism
text:
Transformers and the Attention Mechanism

The transformer is a type of neural network architecture, introduced in 2017, that has become the foundation of nearly all modern language models, including the ones used in retrieval-augmented generation systems. Before transformers, NLP models typically processed text one word at a time, in order, using architectures called recurrent neural networks. This sequential processing was slow and made it difficult for the model to remember information from far earlier in a long piece of text.

The transformer's key innovation is a mechanism called attention. Attention allows the model to look at all the words in a sentence at once and learn which other words are most relevant to understanding each particular word, regardless of how far apart they are in the sentence. For example, in the sentence "The trophy did not fit in the suitcase because it was too big," attention helps the model figure out that "it" most likely refers to the trophy rather than the suitcase, by weighing the relationship between "it" and every other word in the sentence.

A transformer model is typically built from stacked layers, each containing an attention mechanism followed by a simple feed-forward network. By stacking many of these layers, the model builds up increasingly rich and abstract representations of the input text, layer by layer.

Transformer architectures are often described as having two main components: an encoder, which reads and processes an input sequence into a rich internal representation, and a decoder, which generates an output sequence, often one token at a time. Some models use only an encoder (useful for understanding tasks like classification), some use only a decoder (useful for pure text generation), and some use a full encoder-decoder architecture, which is well suited for tasks where an input sequence needs to be transformed into a related but different output sequence, such as translation or generative question answering.

The reason transformers matter so much for a project like this one is that both the embedding model used for retrieval and the generative model used for answering are, under the hood, transformer-based. Understanding attention explains why these models can connect a user's question to relevant information anywhere in a retrieved passage, not just information located near the start.

title: Extractive versus Generative Question Answering
text:
Extractive versus Generative Question Answering

Question answering systems can be broadly divided into two categories based on how they produce their answers: extractive and generative.

An extractive question answering system finds the answer to a question by locating and copying an exact span of text from a source passage. Given a passage of text and a question, the system predicts the start and end position of the answer within that passage, then returns that exact substring as the answer. For example, if a passage states "The Transformer architecture was introduced in 2017," and the question is "When was the Transformer architecture introduced?", an extractive system would identify and return the substring "2017." Extractive systems cannot say anything that is not literally present, word for word, somewhere in the source text.

A generative question answering system works differently. Instead of locating and copying a span of existing text, it uses a language model to compose a brand new answer in natural language. The generative model may draw on relevant source material, often supplied through a retrieval step, but it produces the final wording itself, which means it can paraphrase, combine information from multiple places, summarize, or explain a concept in a way that never appears verbatim anywhere in the source material.

The trade-offs between these two approaches are significant. Extractive QA tends to be more reliable and less prone to inventing false information, since every answer is guaranteed to be a real quote from the source. However, it is inflexible: if the exact answer is not present as a contiguous span of text, an extractive system simply cannot answer well, even if the necessary information is scattered across a passage.

Generative QA is far more flexible and produces answers that read more naturally, since it can synthesize information rather than being limited to copying a single span. This flexibility comes at a cost, however: because the model is composing new text rather than quoting, it can occasionally generate statements that sound fluent and confident but are not actually supported by the source material, a failure mode known as hallucination.

Modern systems increasingly combine both ideas through architectures like retrieval-augmented generation, where a retrieval step first finds the most relevant passages, and a generative model then composes a natural-language answer grounded in that retrieved content. This hybrid approach aims to capture the flexibility of generative answers while reducing the risk of hallucination through explicit grounding in real source text.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
text:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Retrieval-Augmented Generation, commonly abbreviated as RAG, is an architecture that combines a retrieval system with a generative language model in order to produce answers that are grounded in real source documents, rather than relying purely on what the language model happens to have memorized during its training.

A generative language model on its own has two significant weaknesses when used for question answering. First, its knowledge is limited to whatever was present in its training data, which means it will know nothing about documents, facts, or domains that were not part of that training data, such as a specific company's internal documents or a student project's custom knowledge base. Second, when asked something it does not actually know, a language model will often still generate a fluent, confident-sounding answer that is factually wrong, rather than admitting uncertainty. This behavior is called hallucination.

RAG addresses both problems by inserting a retrieval step before generation. When a user asks a question, the system first searches a collection of documents to find the passages most relevant to that question. This search is typically performed using semantic similarity between vector embeddings, rather than simple keyword matching, so that it can find relevant passages even when they are worded very differently from the question itself. The retrieved passages are then inserted into the prompt given to the generative model, alongside the original question, with an instruction to answer using only the provided information.

This approach has several practical benefits. It allows a generative model to answer questions about custom, private, or newly created content without needing to retrain the model itself, since new knowledge can simply be added to the document collection. It also makes answers more auditable, because the system can show which passages were retrieved and used to generate a given answer, letting a user judge for themselves whether the answer is well supported. Finally, because the model is explicitly instructed to rely on the retrieved context, RAG tends to substantially reduce, though not entirely eliminate, the rate of hallucinated answers compared to a generative model working from memory alone.

RAG is not a single fixed algorithm but rather a general architectural pattern, and real systems vary in how they perform retrieval, how many passages they retrieve, whether they rerank retrieved passages before generation, and how the retrieved context is formatted in the prompt. A generative question answering project built around RAG needs to make deliberate, explainable choices at each of these steps.

title: Vector Databases and Document Chunking
text:
Vector Databases and Document Chunking

A vector database, sometimes called a vector store, is a system designed to store large numbers of embedding vectors and efficiently search for the vectors most similar to a given query vector. In a retrieval-augmented generation system, the vector database is what powers the "find relevant passages" step: every document passage is converted into an embedding vector and stored, and when a question arrives, its embedding is compared against all the stored vectors to find the closest matches.

Comparing a query vector against every stored vector one at a time works fine for a small collection, but becomes slow as the collection grows into the thousands or millions of entries. Vector databases use specialized indexing structures and approximate nearest-neighbor search algorithms to make this comparison dramatically faster, trading a small amount of accuracy for a large gain in speed. Popular tools for this purpose include FAISS, a library developed by Meta AI that is widely used in research and student projects because it runs entirely locally, requires no external service, and is straightforward to set up.

Before documents can be embedded and stored, they usually need to be broken into smaller pieces, a process called chunking. Chunking matters for two main reasons. First, embedding models and generative models both have a maximum input length, so a very long document simply cannot be processed as a single unit. Second, and more importantly for answer quality, retrieval works best when each stored piece of text covers a single, focused idea. If an entire long document is stored as one giant chunk, a search might retrieve it because one sentence buried inside is relevant, but the generative model then has to work with a large amount of irrelevant surrounding text, which can dilute the quality of the final answer.

Choosing a chunk size involves a trade-off. Chunks that are too small may cut a single idea in half, losing important context partway through a sentence or explanation. Chunks that are too large reintroduce the problem of diluted, unfocused retrieval results. A common practical approach is to chunk documents into passages of a few hundred tokens each, often with a small amount of overlap between consecutive chunks, so that information near a chunk boundary is not lost entirely from either neighboring chunk.

Once documents are chunked and embedded, the resulting vectors, along with metadata such as which source document and chunk each vector came from, are stored in the vector database. This metadata is what later allows a system to show a user exactly which sources were used to generate a given answer.

title: Hallucination in Generative Language Models
text:
Hallucination in Generative Language Models

In the context of natural language processing, hallucination refers to a situation where a generative language model produces text that is fluent, confident, and grammatically correct, but factually incorrect or entirely unsupported by any real source of information. The term is borrowed loosely from human psychology, since the model is, in a sense, generating a plausible-sounding statement that has no basis in reality, without any internal signal that it is doing so.

Hallucination happens because generative language models are fundamentally trained to predict the next most likely word given the preceding text, based on patterns learned from enormous amounts of training data. When a model is asked something it genuinely does not know, it does not have a built-in mechanism to simply say "I don't know" unless it has been specifically trained or prompted to behave that way. Instead, it tends to produce the most statistically plausible continuation, which can sound entirely convincing while being wrong.

Hallucination is a serious practical problem for any question answering system, because a fluent but incorrect answer can be more dangerous than an obviously broken one: a user has no easy way to tell that the answer is wrong just by reading it. This is especially risky in domains where incorrect information could lead to poor decisions.

Several strategies can help reduce, though not completely eliminate, hallucination. Retrieval-augmented generation is one of the most effective, because it grounds the model's answer in real, retrieved source text rather than relying purely on the model's internal memory. Explicit prompt instructions, such as telling the model to answer only using the provided context and to say that information is unavailable if the answer cannot be found there, further reduce the tendency to invent information. A retrieval relevance threshold can also help: if no retrieved passage is similar enough to the question, the system can decline to answer rather than forcing a generation from weak or irrelevant context. Some systems also display a confidence or relevance score alongside each answer, giving the user a signal of how strongly the answer is supported by the retrieved material.

Measuring hallucination rate is an important part of rigorously evaluating a generative question answering system. This is typically done by testing the system with questions that are deliberately outside its knowledge base, and checking whether it correctly declines to answer rather than inventing a plausible-sounding but false response.

title: Evaluating Question Answering Systems
text:
Evaluating Question Answering Systems

Evaluating a question answering system rigorously requires more than checking whether answers "look right" by eye. Several standard metrics exist, each suited to different kinds of QA systems, and choosing the right ones is an important part of demonstrating that a system actually works.

Exact Match is one of the simplest metrics: it checks whether the generated answer is identical, word for word, to a reference answer. This metric works reasonably well for extractive QA, where the answer is expected to be a specific short span of text, but it is a poor fit for generative QA, since a generative model might produce a correct answer phrased in a completely different way from the reference, and Exact Match would incorrectly score it as wrong.

F1 score, borrowed from classification tasks, measures the overlap between the words in the generated answer and the words in a reference answer, balancing precision (how much of the generated answer is correct) against recall (how much of the reference answer was captured). It is more forgiving than Exact Match, since partial word overlap still counts for something, but it can still unfairly penalize a generative answer that is correct but uses entirely different vocabulary from the reference.

BLEU and ROUGE are metrics originally developed for machine translation and summarization respectively. Both measure overlap of word sequences, called n-grams, between generated and reference text. They can give a rough sense of fluency and content overlap for generated answers, but like Exact Match and F1, they penalize valid paraphrasing.

Semantic similarity metrics take a different approach: instead of comparing exact words, they compare the embedding vectors of the generated answer and the reference answer, and measure how close those vectors are in meaning. This makes semantic similarity much better suited to evaluating generative QA specifically, since a correct answer that is worded completely differently from the reference will still score well, as long as it means the same thing.

For the retrieval half of a RAG system, separate metrics are used. Recall at K measures whether the correct source passage appears somewhere within the top K retrieved results, while Precision at K measures what fraction of the top K retrieved results are actually relevant. These metrics evaluate the retrieval step in isolation from the generation step, which is important because a wrong final answer could be caused either by poor retrieval or by poor generation, and separating the two makes it possible to diagnose which part of the pipeline needs improvement.

Finally, human evaluation, where real people judge the quality, correctness, and helpfulness of generated answers, remains an important complement to automatic metrics, since no single automatic metric perfectly captures everything a human reader would care about, such as clarity, tone, or whether an answer actually resolves the user's underlying question.
